title: The Studio That Redefined Action Animation
excerpt: How a small team of animators turned a niche manga into a global phenomenon, frame by painstaking frame.
body: When the first episode aired, few could have predicted the cultural earthquake that followed. The studio, known until then for modest adaptations and reliable contract work, poured everything into this project — a story about warriors, loss, and the weight of inherited power.

What set the production apart wasn't just the budget. It was the decision to treat every episode like a short film. Action sequences were storyboarded with cinematic intent, with camera moves and pacing borrowed from live-action filmmaking. Animators were given room to inject personal style into key cuts, resulting in episodes that felt wildly different from the uniform look most TV anime settled for.

The result was a show that didn't just look good — it felt alive. Fans dissected frames on social media within hours of each episode going up. Clips circulated far beyond the usual anime circles, pulling in viewers who had never watched a serialized animated series before.

Years later, the ripple effects are still visible. Studios across the industry have raised their standards for action choreography. New productions cite the show as a benchmark. And the team behind it? They went on to found their own studio, taking the philosophy even further.
author: Yuki Tanaka

title: Why Slice-of-Life Anime Hits Different in 2026
excerpt: In a year packed with spectacle, the quietest shows are finding the loudest audiences. Here's why.
body: There's a moment in the season's most talked-about slice-of-life series where two characters sit on a train platform, saying nothing. The camera holds on them for nearly thirty seconds. No music. No inner monologue. Just the sound of a departing train and wind through the platform shelter.

It's the kind of scene that would have been unthinkable a decade ago, when anime was chasing faster cuts and bigger set pieces. But audiences in 2026 are gravitating toward shows that breathe — series that let characters exist in ordinary moments without rushing to the next plot point.

The shift mirrors broader changes in how people consume media. After years of algorithmic feeds and nonstop stimulation, there's a growing appetite for stories that value stillness. Slice-of-life anime, with its emphasis on atmosphere and small emotional beats, fills that gap naturally.

Studios are taking notice. This season alone, six new slice-of-life titles have been announced, several from studios previously known only for action. The genre is no longer a niche — it's becoming the emotional counterweight to an overstimulated era.
author: Mika Sato

title: The Quiet Revolution in Anime Soundtrack Design
excerpt: Composers are blending orchestral traditions with folk instruments and electronic production — and it's changing how we hear anime.
body: Ask anyone to hum an anime theme and they'll probably give you a high-energy J-rock opener. But the most interesting work in anime soundtracks right now isn't happening in the opening credits — it's in the underscore.

A new generation of composers is drawing from unexpected wells: traditional Okinawan folk scales, minimalism in the tradition of Pärt and Glass, even the modular synthesis techniques of Berlin techno. The result is music that doesn't just accompany the visuals but deepens them.

One standout this year is a score built almost entirely around a single folk instrument — a three-stringed lute whose sound most viewers have never consciously heard. The composer used it as a through-line, appearing in different arrangements across twelve episodes, evolving with the protagonist's journey.
It's a reminder that sound design in anime has come a long way from the days of generic synth pads and stock orchestral libraries. The medium is growing up, and its music is growing with it.
author: Ren Kobayashi

title: The Indie Game That Took Six Years and Broke Every Rule
excerpt: A one-person studio shipped a game that critics are calling the best of the decade. The story behind it is even wilder.
body: When the first trailer dropped in 2020, it looked like a student project — rough textures, stiff animations, a UI that seemed placeholder. The developer, working alone from a small apartment, posted it to a forum with the note: "Work in progress. Feedback welcome."

Six years later, that work in progress is a Game of the Year contender. The final product bears only a passing resemblance to that early trailer, but the DNA is the same: a world that reacts to the player in ways no other game does, systems layered on systems until the whole thing feels less like a game and more like a place.

What makes the story remarkable isn't just the solo development — it's the willingness to throw out conventions that every tutorial and every veteran developer would tell you are essential. There's no map. There's no quest log. There's no fast travel. The game trusts the player to find their own way, and rewards curiosity over efficiency.

In an industry increasingly dominated by live-service models and formulaic open worlds, the game's success feels like a quiet rebellion. It proves that there's still room for a single, uncompromising vision — even if it takes six years to deliver.
author: Jordan Lee

title: How Speedrunners Are Keeping a 20-Year-Old Game Alive
excerpt: The community around one classic title has discovered more glitches in the last two years than in the previous eighteen. We talked to the runners pushing the limits.
body: There's a particular moment in any speedrun where the game stops looking like what the developers made and starts looking like something else entirely. A character clips through a wall. A cutscene skips by holding the right buttons during a loading screen. A boss dies in two seconds because of a memory manipulation trick discovered last Tuesday.

For the community around this twenty-year-old classic, those moments are the whole point. What started as a small group trading tips on a forum has grown into a organized scene with regular tournaments, documented strats, and a wiki that runs to thousands of pages.

The pace of discovery has actually accelerated in recent years, thanks to better tools for analysis and a growing community of runners who bring fresh eyes to old problems. "We found more skips in 2025 than in the entire first decade," one runner told us. "The game is still giving us new things to find."
It's a testament to how games can live beyond their release — not through remasters or re-releases, but through the communities that refuse to stop exploring them.
author: Alex Rivera

title: The Best Gaming Soundtracks You Probably Missed
excerpt: Beyond the big-budget orchestral scores, there's a wave of game music that deserves your attention.
body: Everyone knows the iconic themes — the sweeping orchestral scores that play during award ceremonies and end-of-year lists. But some of the most memorable game music of the past year came from games you might not have played.

There's the puzzle game whose entire score is performed on a single prepared piano, with every track corresponding to a game mechanic. There's the RPG that uses a live jazz quintet for its battle themes, shifting to solo cello for its most emotional scenes. And there's the indie platformer whose chiptune soundtrack was composed on original Game Boy hardware.

What connects these scores isn't genre or budget — it's intentionality. Each composer made a deliberate choice about what their game should sound like, and that choice shapes the experience as much as any visual or mechanic.
If you've been sleeping on game music beyond the headline titles, this is your wake-up call. The medium is producing some of the most adventurous composition happening anywhere right now.
author: Sam Chen

title: The Spice and the Sand: How Denis Villeneuve Mastered Dune: Part Two
excerpt: From infrared desert cameras in Jordan to Hans Zimmer's otherworldly score, Denis Villeneuve transformed Frank Herbert's epic into cinema history.
body: When the lights dimmed for Dune: Part Two, audiences were greeted not with a standard Hollywood sequel, but with an uncompromising, visceral monument of visual storytelling. Denis Villeneuve took the deliberate world-building of the 2021 film and ignited it into a sweeping, terrifying examination of religious fundamentalism, power, and destiny.

Cinematographer Greig Fraser utilized specialized infrared cameras to capture the blinding, desolate glare of the Arrakis sun across the dunes of Jordan and Abu Dhabi. The resulting imagery stripped away color in favor of stark, radiant white sands and obsidian shadows, giving the Fremen guerrilla campaign an almost tactile reality.

At the center of this triumph is Timothée Chalamet's metamorphosis from a grieving young prince into the chilling, prescient warlord Muad'Dib. Paired with Zendaya's grounded, skeptical Chani and Austin Butler's psychopathic Feyd-Rautha, the film avoids standard savior tropes to deliver a deeply unsettling cautionary tale.

With over $714 million at the global box office and near-unanimous critical acclaim, Dune: Part Two proved that audiences are hungry for auteur-driven, high-concept science fiction when handled with complete technical mastery and thematic ambition.
author: Marcus Webb

title: Breaking the Canon: Inside the Groundbreaking Visuals of Across the Spider-Verse
excerpt: Six animation styles, 240 distinct characters, and a multiverse of color: how Sony Pictures Animation revolutionized comic book cinema.
body: Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse pushed the boundaries of animated filmmaking further than any feature in modern memory. Rather than adopting a singular aesthetic, directors Joaquim Dos Santos, Kemp Powers, and Justin K. Thompson constructed an entire visual language tailored to each dimension.

From the bleeding watercolor expressionism of Gwen Stacy's Earth-65—where backgrounds shift hue to reflect her inner emotional turbulence—to the retro-futuristic Syd Mead-inspired towers of Nueva York (Earth-928), every frame is packed with custom artistic flourishes and handcrafted line art.

The film required over 1,000 animators and revolutionized software pipelines to allow disparate styles—such as Daniel Kaluuya's punk-rock collage Spider-Punk (Hobie Brown)—to exist in the same frame without feeling disjointed.

Beyond the visual pyrotechnics, Across the Spider-Verse resonates because of Miles Morales' refusal to accept predetermined tragedy. By questioning the very concept of 'canon events', the film challenges decades of comic book storytelling and cements itself as a modern classic.
author: Elena Rossi

title: Shadows, Rain, and Rage: The Neo-Noir Architecture of The Batman
excerpt: Matt Reeves and Greig Fraser stripped the superhero myth down to a rain-soaked 1970s detective thriller, redefining Gotham City.
body: In a superhero landscape saturated with multiversal stakes and world-ending skybeams, Matt Reeves' The Batman dared to be something radically different: a grounded, psychological detective procedural steeped in the traditions of All the President's Men, Klute, and Se7en.

Robert Pattinson's Bruce Wayne is not an invincible playboy, but a nocturnal recluse still consumed by grief and early in his crusade. Operating from a gritty, rusted Batcave beneath Wayne Tower, his journey forces him to confront the realization that raw vengeance only breeds greater chaos.

Greig Fraser's Oscar-nominated cinematography combined custom anamorphic lenses with silhouetted orange flares, perpetual drizzle, and deep obsidian shadows to make Gotham feel like a living, decaying metropolis rather than a studio backdrop.
With The Batman Part II scheduled for 2026, the groundwork laid here remains one of the most distinctive, stylish interpretations of comic book lore ever brought to the silver screen.
author: David Park

title: The Quantum Reckoning: Christopher Nolan and the Physical Terror of Oppenheimer
excerpt: Zero CGI, real magnesium explosions, and 11-mile IMAX film reels: inside the monumental craft behind Oppenheimer.
body: Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer achieved what many deemed impossible: turning a three-hour biographical drama about theoretical physicists and bureaucratic hearings into a billion-dollar global cinematic event.

By steadfastly refusing to use computer-generated imagery for the Trinity test, Nolan and supervisor Andrew Jackson created miniature chemical reactions, forced-perspective magnesium bursts, and high-speed photography to evoke the cosmic horror of splitting the atom.

Cillian Murphy's haunting, hollowed-out portrayal of J. Robert Oppenheimer is anchored by Ludwig Göransson's relentless violin score and Hoyte van Hoytema's monumental IMAX 70mm large-format portraiture, which turned human faces into dramatic landscapes.
Sweeping seven Academy Awards including Best Picture and Best Director, Oppenheimer reaffirmed the cultural vitality of theatrical, adult-oriented cinematic storytelling.
author: Sarah Lin

title: Colosseum Reborn: Ridley Scott and the Savage Grandeur of Gladiator II
excerpt: Twenty-four years after the original Oscar triumph, Ridley Scott returns to ancient Rome with Paul Mescal and Denzel Washington.
body: More than two decades after Russell Crowe's Maximus Decimus Meridius took his final breath on the sands of the Colosseum, director Ridley Scott returns to ancient Rome with Gladiator II.

Starring Paul Mescal as an adult Lucius Aurelius, the film picks up decades after the fall of Commodus, finding Rome under the tyrannical grip of dual emperors Caracalla and Geta. Captured in northern Africa, Lucius is forced into the arena under the ruthless tutelage of arms merchant Macrinus, played with electric ferocity by Denzel Washington.
Scott utilizes unprecedented scale, staging full naval battles inside a flooded Colosseum, vicious rhino gladiatorial combat, and massive Roman legions in siege warfare.
Gladiator II bridges visceral practical action with Shakespearean palace intrigue, proving that the sword-and-sandal historical epic still holds an unmatched power on the big screen.
author: Julian Thorne

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day - The Clean Slate Era of Peter Parker
excerpt: Forgotten by the world and operating alone on the streets of New York, Tom Holland's Peter Parker enters his darkest, most grounded journey.
body: Following the tragic climax of No Way Home, where Doctor Strange's spell erased Peter Parker from the memories of everyone he loves, the Marvel Cinematic Universe is preparing for a new, grounded era in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

Stripped of Stark tech, Avengers support, and high-society billionaire alliances, Peter Parker is once again the street-level hero fans have yearned for: living in a cramped rundown Manhattan apartment, sewing his own suits, and listening to police scanners.

Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, Brand New Day introduces new allies and gritty mob syndicates, setting Peter on a collision course with street-level crime that tests whether he can endure the cost of his solitary crusade.
Scheduled for release in 2026, Brand New Day marks a vital transition for the web-slinger, combining classic comic book roots with mature, character-driven storytelling.
author: Yuki Tanaka

title: The Golden Age of Limited Series
excerpt: The one-season story is becoming the dominant form of prestige television — and it's changing how writers think about structure.
body: For a decade, the default ambition of any serious TV show was to run as long as possible. Five seasons, seven seasons, ten — the thinking was that longevity equaled significance. But the limited series has quietly overtaken the multi-season drama as the form where the best writing is happening.

The reasons are practical as much as creative. Audiences are more willing to commit to a story with a clear endpoint. Platforms like the marketing hook of a self-contained event. And writers, freed from the need to sustain a premise indefinitely, can build stories with actual shape — beginning, middle, end.

The best limited series this year feel like novels. Six to eight episodes, each one essential, no filler, no wheel-spinning. The form demands discipline: every scene has to earn its place because there's no next season to compensate for a weak episode.

It's also attracting talent that wouldn't have touched television a decade ago. Film directors, literary writers, theater actors — the limited series has become the prestige format, the place where you can tell a complete story with the resources and reach of television.
author: Rachel Green

title: How Streaming Changed the Way We Rewatch
excerpt: The comfort rewatch is now a defining viewing habit. What does it tell us about how audiences relate to television?
body: There was a time when rewatching a show meant catching reruns in syndication, episodes out of order, edited for time. Streaming changed that. Now, the entire series is always there — and audiences are using that access in ways the industry didn't predict.

The comfort rewatch — returning to a familiar show not for plot surprises but for the pleasure of spending time with characters you know — has become one of the most common viewing patterns. For some platforms, rewatch hours make up the majority of total watch time.

It tells us something about the role television plays in people's lives. A new show is a commitment, a risk. A familiar show is a known quantity, a warm room you can walk into. In a media landscape that constantly demands attention to the new, the comfort rewatch is a form of rest.

Writers and showrunners are noticing. Some are building shows designed to reward rewatching — planting details that only land on a second pass, writing episodes that feel different once you know where the story goes. The rewatch isn't a side effect anymore. It's part of the design.
author: Tom Wilson

title: The TV Soundtrack Renaissance Nobody Is Talking About
excerpt: From needle drops to original scores, television music has never been more ambitious.
body: Television music used to be functional: a theme song, some library cues, maybe a licensed track for a key moment. No one talked about the score of a TV show the way they talked about a film score. That's changed.

This year's standout shows feature scores that rival any film composition. One drama built its entire sound around a custom-built instrument — a wall of tuned percussion that gives every scene a unique, otherworldly quality. Another used a string quartet recorded in a reverberant church, creating a sound that's intimate and enormous at the same time.

The needle drop has evolved too. Where shows once used popular songs as emotional shorthand, the best shows now use them as structural elements — a song that recurs across episodes, changing meaning each time it appears. A track that plays diegetically in one scene and returns as score in another.

Television has more time than film — more room to develop musical ideas, to let a motif evolve across hours rather than minutes. The composers who understand that are creating some of the most compelling music in any medium.
author: Lisa Chang

title: The Choreography That Broke the Internet
excerpt: A 40-second dance challenge became the year's biggest cultural moment. We talked to the choreographer who created it.
body: It started as a fan cam — a vertical video, ten seconds long, posted from a music show recording. By the end of the week, it had been viewed hundreds of millions of times. Within a month, the dance challenge had been attempted by everyone from professional dancers to world leaders.

The choreographer behind it has been working in K-pop for over a decade, creating routines for some of the industry's biggest groups. But nothing they'd done before prepared them for this. "I knew the move was catchy," they told us. "I didn't know it would become this."

What makes the choreography work isn't complexity — it's the opposite. The key move is simple enough that anyone can attempt it, but distinctive enough that it immediately reads as belonging to this song and this group. It's a balance that K-pop choreography has been refining for years.

The challenge has also opened a broader conversation about how dance functions in the age of short-form video. A great chorus used to be the hook; now, a great move might matter just as much. The industry is paying attention.
author: Ji-ho Kim

title: How Fan Culture Shapes K-Pop Comebacks
excerpt: From streaming parties to fan-made merch, the relationship between groups and their fans has evolved into something unlike anything else in music.
body: In K-pop, a comeback isn't just a release — it's an event, coordinated between label, group, and fans with a precision that would impress a military strategist. Fan communities organize streaming goals, voting campaigns, and social media pushes that can shape chart positions in real time.

What's remarkable is how this relationship has formalized. Fan bases operate with structured teams, designated roles, and communication channels that can mobilize thousands of people within minutes. Labels have noticed — some now incorporate fan feedback into promotion strategies, timing teasers and content drops to align with fan activity patterns.

The line between audience and participant has blurred. Fans don't just consume the content — they create it: edits, covers, fan art, analysis videos that sometimes reach more viewers than the official content. The most engaged fan communities function almost as extensions of the promotional apparatus.

It raises questions about sustainability and boundaries, which the industry is still working through. But there's no question that the K-pop model — where the relationship between artist and fan is treated as the core product, not a byproduct — has reshaped what a music release can be.
author: Min-ji Park

title: The Producers Behind the Year's Biggest K-Pop Hits
excerpt: A new wave of producers is reshaping the K-pop sound — blending global influences with the genre's distinctive energy.
body: Ask a K-pop fan to name their favorite producer and you might be surprised by how quickly they answer. In an industry that used to keep its creative teams behind the scenes, producers have become names in their own right — credited, discussed, anticipated.

This year's biggest hits come from a diverse group of producers, several of whom came to K-pop from other genres — UK garage, Latin pop, American R&B. What they bring isn't just new sounds but new structural approaches: songs that break the verse-chorus-verse template, that build to unexpected drops, that reference genres K-pop hasn't traditionally touched.

The collaborations have gone global too. Producers from Stockholm, Seoul, and Los Angeles working on the same track, each bringing their regional sensibility. The result is a sound that's simultaneously more specific and more universal — unmistakably K-pop, but drawing from a wider palette than ever.

For a genre that has always thrived on synthesis, this new chapter feels like a natural evolution. K-pop has never been about purity. It's about taking the best parts of everything and making them move together.
author: Soo-young Lee

title: The Indie Comic That Started as a Webcomic and Became a Phenomenon
excerpt: A free webcomic became the year's best-selling graphic novel. The creator still can't quite believe it.
body: It started as a side project — a few pages posted online every month, drawn in the creator's spare time between freelance illustration jobs. No publisher, no marketing, no plan beyond "I want to tell this story."

Three years later, those pages have been collected into a graphic novel that debuted at the top of bestseller lists. The print run sold out in a week. A film adaptation is in development. And the creator is still updating the webcomic for free, posting new pages on the same schedule they always have.

What resonated with readers isn't easy to pin down. The art is distinctive — a style that doesn't look like anything else on the shelf — but it's the storytelling that kept people coming back. A story about identity and belonging, told with a specificity that makes the personal feel universal.

The success has also highlighted a shift in how comics reach audiences. Webcomics, once seen as a stepping stone to "real" publication, have become a legitimate endpoint. For creators who want to own their work and reach readers directly, the webcomic-to-print model offers a path that didn't exist a decade ago.
author: Chris Miller

title: Why Comic Lettering Matters More Than You Think
excerpt: It's the invisible art of comics — the thing you only notice when it's wrong. We talked to three letterers about their craft.
body: If you've never thought about comic lettering, you're not alone. It's the element of comics that's designed to be transparent — to deliver the words without calling attention to itself. But the letterers who do it well are some of the most skilled craftspeople in the medium.

Good lettering is about more than readable fonts. It's about pacing — how a balloon's placement guides the reader's eye through the page. It's about character — how a villain's speech looks different from a hero's. It's about emphasis — how bold, italic, and size changes tell the reader how to "hear" the words.
"The best lettering is lettering you don't notice," one letterer told us. "If the reader is thinking about the balloon shapes, they're not in the story. My job is to disappear."

The craft has evolved with technology. Digital tools have made lettering more precise and flexible, but the fundamental decisions — where to place a balloon, how to shape a tail, when to use a burst balloon — remain matters of instinct and taste. It's a reminder that comics are a collaborative medium, and every credit on the page matters.
author: Nate Brooks

title: The Evolution of the Superhero Costume
excerpt: From spandex to tactical armor to something in between — how superhero design has reflected the times for eighty years.
body: The superhero costume is one of the most recognizable design languages in popular culture. But it's never been static. The costume that worked in the 1940s wouldn't work today — not because it looks dated (though it does), but because it was designed for a different context.

Early costumes were about clarity: bold colors, simple shapes, silhouettes that read instantly even in cheap newsprint. As printing improved, costumes gained detail — musculature, texture, accessories that told you something about the character. The 90s brought pouches and shoulder pads, reflecting the era's aesthetic excess. The 2000s brought tactical reimagining — armor, straps, functional design that treated superheroes as people who might actually need protection.

The current era is something more fluid. Costumes are being designed with movement in mind — how they look in action, how they communicate character through posture and gesture. Some of the most interesting recent designs are deconstructions: costumes that reference the classic look while commenting on it, acknowledging that a character who's been around for sixty years has a relationship with their own visual identity.

The best costume designers understand that a superhero's outfit isn't just clothing — it's a statement about who the character is and what world they inhabit. The costume is the story before the story begins.
author: Grace Liu

title: The Manga That Refuses to End (And Why That's Okay)
excerpt: Some series run for decades. We look at what keeps a long-running manga vital when most stories would have run out of steam.
body: There's a particular kind of anxiety that sets in when a manga you love enters its tenth year. Will it overstay its welcome? Will the author run out of things to say? The history of manga is full of series that went on too long, diluting their legacy with years of diminishing returns.

But there are a handful of series that have been running for decades and are still producing some of their best work. How? The answer, it turns out, isn't about maintaining momentum — it's about evolving.

The best long-running manga don't try to sustain their original premise indefinitely. They let their characters age, their worlds change, their themes deepen. A series that started as a simple adventure becomes a meditation on responsibility. A comedy develops real emotional stakes. The story grows up with its readers.

It requires a particular kind of confidence from the author — the willingness to let the story become something different from what it started as, to risk alienating readers who loved the early version. But when it works, the result is something unique to manga: a story that has the scope of a life.
author: Kenji Mori

title: The Ink That Tells the Story: Manga Art Techniques
excerpt: Screentone, brushwork, panel layout — the tools that make manga a distinct visual language.
body: Manga is a black-and-white medium. That limitation has produced one of the most sophisticated visual languages in all of comics — a system of techniques built to convey everything that color does, using only ink on paper.

Screentone — the adhesive sheets of dot patterns that manga artists apply to create gradients, textures, and shading — is perhaps the most recognizable technique. Though many artists now work digitally, the aesthetic of screentone remains fundamental to how manga looks. The choice of dot pattern, its density, its placement — all carry meaning.

Brushwork is the other pillar. The way an artist handles ink — the thickness of lines, the energy of brush strokes, the contrast between detailed and spare areas — defines their style as clearly as a signature. Some artists work in a clean, precise line; others use brush and pen to create pages that feel almost painterly.

Panel layout is where it all comes together. Manga is famous for its adventurous page compositions — panels that bleed into each other, pages dominated by a single image, layouts that control pacing by controlling how the eye moves. It's a reminder that manga isn't just illustrated fiction. It's a medium with its own grammar.
author: Aoi Hashimoto

title: Weekly serialization vs Monthly: How Publishing Shapes Story
excerpt: The pace at which a manga is published changes everything about how its story is told.
body: A weekly manga author draws about twenty pages every seven days. A monthly author draws about forty pages every thirty days. The difference in page count is significant — but the difference in storytelling approach is even more profound.

Weekly serialization rewards momentum. Each chapter needs a hook — a cliffhanger, a reveal, a moment that brings the reader back next week. The pace is relentless, and it shapes the kind of stories that work: action-driven, plot-forward, with characters and conflicts that can sustain constant movement. There's little room for quiet chapters or slow development.

Monthly serialization allows for a different rhythm. With more pages per chapter and more time between them, authors can build scenes that breathe. A monthly chapter might spend its entire length on a single conversation, a single fight, a single moment of introspection — and it can do so without feeling slow, because the reader knows the next installment is a month away, not a week.

Neither format is inherently better. Some stories need the urgency of weekly publication; others need the space of monthly. But understanding the difference helps explain why two manga, both excellent, can feel so fundamentally different in their pacing and structure.
author: Ryo Saito
